_notes: PAGES THE PROLOGUE REACHES BY SITUATION, NOT BY INDEX.
The Hollow Court is played as a small SCENE rather than one wall of
text (owner 2026-08-04: the first visit read as if Ash already knew
the place). Lives are spent, never taken (owner 2026-08-11,
docs/design/death-and-lives.md): hollow_court_first and _repeat are
TRUE deaths only -- authored `mortal` beats, one countdown visit per
life, each seen at most once. hollow_court_refused is every ordinary
defeat: the Court refusing an unscheduled death. Its first entry
teaches; the rest rotate (law 15). TWO refused variants carry planted
clues -- read docs/design/the-unraveler.md before editing ANY of them.
mantel_coach walks the room once, the first time it is entered.
unpicked_won is the scene for beating a fight that is not meant to be
winnable -- it exists because somebody will.
A THIRD PLANTED CLUE lives in hollow_court_first, not in the refusal
rotation, so the one-hint-per-refusal-batch budget is untouched: the
Clerk reaches the posting line for Ash's first appointment and finds it
BLANK. Somebody booked that death and did not sign for it. Literally
true, unremarked, and it re-reads in Ch3 (novel/story-bible/03-timeline
.md: Bodkin posts Ash's death as an appointment, the gentlest slot on the
ledger). Do not have the Clerk notice it aloud -- he must not deduce
before the player can.

lines: The cold goes first. Then the noise. Then the part of me that was worried about the noise.
What is left over is standing in a corridor that is all filing and no building, under a ceiling too far up to be a ceiling.
Nothing hurts. I would like it on record that I find this deeply suspicious.

hollow_court_first.art_desc: The Hollow Court: a translucent clerk at a lamplit desk before endless filing shelves, one empty chair facing him
lines: A desk. A lamp. A queue of one, and the one is me.
The Clerk does not look up. 'Name?'
answers: 'Everyone here is something.' He turns a page without touching it, and then stops turning it.

'Nine.' He looks at me over the spectacles for the first time. 'You have NINE.' He checks the sheet again, and then a second sheet, and his face does what a clerk's face does when the arithmetic is somebody else's problem.
'...Vane's familiar. Well. That is what it says.' He writes it down exactly as written. 'Nine allotted. One spent.'
'Needle Lane.' Something moves behind the spectacles that is almost interest. 'Yes. We have had a busy evening from Needle Lane.'
Then he reaches the column that matters and stops. 'Nine allotted.' He says it to the paper, not to me. 'I have not filed a nine since I was at a much smaller desk.'
'Vane's familiar. One spent.' He does not say whose the busy evening was. I do not ask. Not here.
The silence goes on long enough to become a position. He allows it, and writes anyway.
Halfway down he stops. 'Nine,' he says, to nobody. He turns the sheet over as though the back might explain it. It does not.
'Vane's familiar. Nine allotted, one spent.' — 'You will find that not answering is also an answer, and that I have a great deal of filing.'

lines: 'The arrangement, since it is your first: deaths are appointments. Tonight you had one.' He says it the way a man reads weather. Then he looks at the column beside it, where the posting line is, and where the name of whoever posted the appointment goes.
It is blank. He does not remark on it. He writes nothing in it, either.
'Arrive dead WITHOUT an appointment and you will be refused at this desk — we are a court, not a revolving door.'

lines.text: A true death — the kind you will always see coming — costs a life. After the first, it also costs the Toll: a quarter of the shine banked at home. Any other defeat is REFUSED: no life spent, a filing fee of one part in ten from the bank. Either way the satchel stays where you dropped it, and nothing else is ever lost — not your kit, not your case, not what you have worked out.

lines: 'The first visit is complimentary. Do consider it a courtesy rather than a habit.'
The stamp comes down. It is, I notice, a paw print. Neither of us remarks on this.

hollow_court_first.art_desc: A narrow stone stair climbing out of the Hollow Court's filing dark towards a small warm doorway far above, one black cat starting up it
lines: The stairs up are longer
than the fall down.
They always are.
The desk again. The lamp again. He does not look up.
'Back so soon. The form remembers you, which saves us both time.'
The Toll is taken. Professionally. Almost gently.

hollow_court_repeat.art_desc: Extreme close on the Clerk's hand bringing the stamp down; the impression already on the paper is an inked cat paw print
lines: Third. He has the stamp out before I reach the chair, which I choose to find efficient rather than insulting.
'You are making a habit of an arrangement,' he says. 'Habits are how arrangements become entitlements. I mention it only professionally.'
I sit anyway. He lets me.
'Four,' says the Clerk, and for once does not write it down immediately.
'May I ask what you are doing up there?' — I am looking for someone. — 'Ah. Yes. That is the usual answer, and the usual number of lives it takes.'
The stamp comes down softer than it needs to.
He has started keeping my file on the desk rather than in the drawer. Out is worse than filed; he told me so himself, once.
'Halfway,' he says. Not unkindly. That is the trouble with him.
'I am obliged to remind you that the allotment is not a budget. It is a quantity of you.'

hollow_court_repeat.art_desc: The Hollow Court desk exactly as always, with one addition nobody mentions: a second chair, exactly cat-sized, beside the full-size one
lines: There is a chair at the desk that was not there before. It is exactly cat-sized. Neither of us mentions it.
'The Toll,' he says, and takes it, and then sits with his hands folded for a moment longer than the work requires.
'Go carefully. That is not in the form. I am saying it anyway.'
He counts what is left twice. He is not a man who counts twice.
'Two,' he says. 'You will want to know what happens at nought. It is not dramatic. The file closes and the desk is empty and there is a great deal of filing that afternoon.'
'I would rather not do the filing.'

hollow_court_repeat.art_desc: The Hollow Court desk with the lamp turned up bright and warm, shadows pushed back, one file lying open on the desk
lines: The lamp is turned up. He has turned the lamp up, for me, which is the most alarming thing that has happened tonight.
'One,' says the Clerk. 'I will not lecture you. You know precisely what you are spending and precisely what you are spending it on.'
'Whatever it is up there — do finish it.'

hollow_court_refused.art_desc: Extreme close on the Clerk's hand bringing the stamp down; the impression already on the paper is an inked cat paw print
lines: The corridor. The filing. The desk. I appear to be dead — and the Clerk is already shaking his head.
'You are not on the docket.' He holds the sheet up as proof. 'No appointment, no death. We do not process walk-ins.'

lines.text: A defeat off the docket spends no life. You are sent back up, minus a tenth-part filing fee and whatever the satchel held. A true death is always announced. This was not one.

lines: The stamp says REFUSED. It is also, somehow, still a paw print.
'Still not on the docket,' he says, before I have reached the chair.
'There is a folder for these now. IRREGULAR, it says on the cover. It is becoming a thick folder, and thick folders attract auditors.'
The fee is taken. The stamp, I notice, was inked before I arrived.

hollow_court_refused.art_desc: The Clerk running a length of fine silver thread through his fingers, the same thread laid along a ruled line in the open ledger that is plainly too short for it
lines: He has my thread out on the desk, laid along a ruled line in the ledger. The ruled line is shorter.
'You have arrived with more thread than my arithmetic says you left with. I have written CLERICAL ERROR.' He looks at the words a while. 'I do not write fiction, as a rule.'
REFUSED, says the stamp, with feeling.

hollow_court_refused.art_desc: A queue of translucent grey ghosts at the Hollow Court desk, turning to wave a small black cat forward to the front of the line
lines: There is a queue tonight. The queue is ghosts, and the ghosts wave me forward, which I find polite and insulting in equal parts.
'No appointment under your name,' says the Clerk. 'The docket is beginning to feel strongly about you.'
Back up the stairs. They are no shorter for the practice.

hollow_court_refused.art_desc: The Clerk stopped mid-stamp with the thread run through his fingers, spectacles down, finding a knot that is not one of theirs
lines: He stops mid-stamp, spectacles down, and runs my thread through his fingers, slowly.
'There is a knot here that is not one of ours,' he says. 'Close work. Old-fashioned. Whoever ties these does not care to have them noticed.' He files nothing. He remembers it, though. So do I.
The stamp comes down late. REFUSED, as ever.
'One day,' says the Clerk, 'you will arrive here properly, with an appointment. I confess I do not look forward to the filing.'
'Until then: the fee, the stamp, the stairs. You know the way better than some of my staff.'
The stairs. Again. Up.

mantel_coach.text: Her parlor. Cold, and still hers. This is where a night begins and, with luck, ends.
What the city wants doing gets pinned to the chimney breast. One thing tonight.
Tap a note to take the work. Backing out costs nothing — the board is a board of choices.
Gleam. Buttons, mostly, and the occasional tooth. It buys cards, and it is what the Court takes when you die. Out on a job it rides in the SATCHEL.
Lives, the spool, and deeds recorded. Watch the spool: it does not refill while you are out. Tap the deeds to leaf through them.
The Casebook: everything I know. On the Prowl: what I carry out the door — claws and spool both. More along this wall when I have reason.

unpicked_won: It comes apart. Thread by thread. That was not supposed to happen.
Somewhere below the city, a clerk files something under 'irregular'.
